desc: ODNI was created by the Intelligence Reform and Terrorism Prevention Act of 2004 (Public Law 108-458) and stood up on 22 April 2005, placing a Director of National Intelligence above the Intelligence Community elements that had previously answered to the Director of Central Intelligence. For the UAP record ODNI is the co-author of the modern disclosure regime: the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence's report accompanying the Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2021 directed the DNI, in consultation with the Secretary of Defense, to deliver a report on unidentified aerial phenomena, and on 25 June 2021 ODNI published 'Preliminary Assessment: Unidentified Aerial Phenomena'. That nine-page document analysed 144 reports from USG sources, of which 80 involved multiple sensors, and sorted them into five explanatory categories - airborne clutter, natural atmospheric phenomena, USG or U.S. industry developmental programs, foreign adversary systems, and a catch-all 'other'. Its contributor list is itself an intelligence product: USD(I&S), DIA, FBI, NRO, NGA, NSA, the Air Force, the Army, the Navy and ONI, DARPA, FAA, NOAA, ODNI's National Intelligence Manager for Emerging and Disruptive Technology, the National Counterintelligence and Security Center and the National Intelligence Council. ODNI thereafter became a statutory annual reporter on UAP under successive intelligence authorisation acts and NDAAs, and it is one of the four agencies whose records NARA identified in its 24 April 2025 release into the statutory UAP Collection. ODNI is also the parent of the Intelligence Community Inspector General, whose finding that David Grusch's complaint was 'credible and urgent' is the single most consequential procedural act in the modern record.

claims.text: The 25 June 2021 'Preliminary Assessment: Unidentified Aerial Phenomena' was produced by ODNI in response to a provision in Senate Report 116-233 accompanying the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021, directing the DNI in consultation with the Secretary of Defense to assess the threat posed by UAP and the UAPTF's progress.

The assessment states it 'was drafted by the UAPTF and the ODNI National Intelligence Manager for Aviation, with input from USD(I&S), DIA, FBI, NRO, NGA, NSA, Air Force, Army, Navy, Marine Corps, DARPA, FAA, NASA, NOAA, ODNI/NIM-Emerging and Disruptive Technology, ODNI/National Counterintelligence and Security Center, and ODNI/National Intelligence Council.'

The assessment states: 'Most of the UAP reported probably do represent physical objects given that a majority of UAP registered across multiple sensors, to include radar, infrared, electro-optical, weapon seekers, and visual observation.'
The assessment states: 'The UAPTF has 11 reports of documented instances in which pilots reported near misses with a UAP.'

On the possibility that UAP are US black programs the assessment states: 'Some UAP observations could be attributable to classified USG aerospace programs or systems under development by commercial aerospace firms. We were unable to confirm, however, that these systems accounted for any of the UAP reports we collected.'
The assessment states: 'The UAPTF had no MASINT reporting on the events considered in this dataset.'

The assessment defines five explanatory categories into which resolved UAP incidents would fall: airborne clutter, natural atmospheric phenomena, USG or U.S. industry developmental programs, foreign adversary systems, and a catchall 'other' bin.
The dataset described in the assessment 'is currently limited primarily to USG reporting of incidents occurring from November 2004 to March 2021.'

The FOIA-released version of the assessment, approved for release by ODNI on 24 March 2022 under case DF-2021-00275, withholds material under exemptions (b)(1) and (b)(3), including the name of the UAPTF Director identified in the text as 'the official accountable for ensuring the timely collection and consolidation of data on UAP,' redacted under (b)(3) and (b)(6).
The assessment notes 'some UAP have been detected near military facilities or by aircraft carrying the USG's most advanced sensor systems.'

DoD Directive 5205.07, effective 12 September 2024 and approved by Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen H. Hicks, designates USD(I&S) as the office that 'serves as the primary interface for the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) and members of the Intelligence Community (IC), including sharing with the DoD compartmented capabilities and information intended for inclusion and subsequent apportionment' — the same office in which AARO is housed.

50 U.S.C. 3373 requires the Secretary of Defense, in coordination with the Director of National Intelligence, to establish the office known as the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office, and requires the secure UAP reporting mechanism to be established in consultation with the DNI.

In 2022 Intelligence Community Inspector General Thomas Monheim found David Grusch's PPD-19 urgent-concern complaint credible and urgent, and a summary was transmitted to the Director of National Intelligence and to the House and Senate intelligence committees; Grusch subsequently testified publicly to House Oversight in July 2023.

Michael Shellenberger's November 2024 congressional testimony quotes DNI John Ratcliffe stating in 2021 that UAP demonstrated 'technologies that we don't have and, frankly, that we are not capable of defending against,' that analysts had 'high confidence' foreign adversaries were not behind the Tic Tac encounter, and that 'there are a lot more sightings than have been made public.'

The Fiscal Year 2024 Consolidated Annual Report on Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena, released 14 November 2024 and carried on the ODNI website, reports 757 UAP reports received, of which 485 occurred within the reporting period and 272 occurred in 2021-2022 but were reported late; 118 cases were resolved to prosaic objects and 21 remain unexplained.

Sections 1841-1843 of the FY2024 NDAA, now codified at 44 U.S.C. 2107 note, require NARA to establish the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection consisting of 'copies of all Government, Government-provided, or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence'; NARA established Record Group 615 for it, creating a statutory transfer obligation that reaches every IC element ODNI coordinates.

connections: ODNI to UAPTF to AARO: the same reporting lineage, with ODNI's National Intelligence Manager for Aviation as the drafting office in 2021 and AARO now lodged inside OUSD(I&S), ODNI's designated DoD interface under DoDD 5205.07.

The 2021 drafting roster names every agency with a UAP equity as of that date — DIA, FBI, NRO, NGA, NSA, DARPA, FAA, NASA, NOAA, NCSC, NIC — and is therefore a target list for NARA Record Group 615 transfer compliance.
The redacted UAPTF Director's name under (b)(6) is a specific, resolvable identity gap; the same office is the accountability node the Senate report demanded be identified.

ICIG Thomas Monheim to DNI Avril Haines to the congressional intelligence committees is the documented Grusch referral path; the substance of what ODNI did with it is unaddressed in any public product.

The assessment's statement that the UAPTF had no MASINT reporting sits in direct conflict with the Immaculate Constellation allegation that a parent USAP holds high-quality IMINT and MASINT — either the UAPTF was walled off from that collection, or one of the two statements is false.

DNI John Ratcliffe's 2021 public statements are the most permissive on-record remarks by any DNI and are quoted into the congressional record by a November 2024 witness; DNI succession since (Haines, Gabbard, Clayton) is a change-of-posture axis worth tracking.
Michael Gold's testimony connects ODNI's collection problem to NASA's Aviation Safety Reporting System and to CNES/GEIPAN as civil-side data sources the IC has not integrated.
dossier.denialPosture: ODNI has never denied that a legacy retrieval or reverse-engineering program exists; it has denied confirmation. Its 2021 assessment states it was 'unable to confirm' that US classified aerospace programs accounted for any collected UAP report, and that it 'currently lacks data' to attribute UAP to a foreign collection program. The characteristic ODNI posture is epistemic hedging plus redaction, not categorical denial — which is a materially different artifact from the flat DoD denials on this board.
dossier.narrative:
ODNI's formal entry into the UAP file came through an appropriations rider rather than through the intelligence community's own initiative. Senate Report 116-233, accompanying the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021, directed the DNI, in consultation with the Secretary of Defense, to submit an intelligence assessment of the threat posed by unidentified aerial phenomena and of the progress the Department of Defense Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force had made in understanding it. The resulting nine-page unclassified 'Preliminary Assessment: Unidentified Aerial Phenomena,' dated 25 June 2021, is the single most-cited government document on the subject, and it repays close reading of the FOIA copy rather than the sanitised public one.

The drafting roster alone is analytically valuable. The report was 'drafted by the UAPTF and the ODNI National Intelligence Manager for Aviation, with input from USD(I&S), DIA, FBI, NRO, NGA, NSA, Air Force, Army, Navy, Marine Corps, DARPA, FAA, NASA, NOAA, ODNI/NIM-Emerging and Disruptive Technology, ODNI/National Counterintelligence and Security Center, and ODNI/National Intelligence Council.' That is a list of every organisation with an equity in the file as of 2021, and it is a map of where records exist.

The substantive findings are hedged but not empty. 'Most of the UAP reported probably do represent physical objects given that a majority of UAP registered across multiple sensors, to include radar, infrared, electro-optical, weapon seekers, and visual observation.' The UAPTF 'has 11 reports of documented instances in which pilots reported near misses with a UAP.' The dataset is limited primarily to US government reporting of incidents from November 2004 to March 2021. The report proposes five explanatory bins — airborne clutter, natural atmospheric phenomena, USG or US industry developmental programs, foreign adversary systems, and a catchall 'other' — and then, on the third bin, delivers the sentence a program hypothesis must build on: 'Some UAP observations could be attributable to classified USG aerospace programs or systems under development by commercial aerospace firms. We were unable to confirm, however, that these systems accounted for any of the UAP reports we collected.' On foreign adversaries: 'We currently lack data to determine any UAP are part of a foreign collection program or indicative of a major technological advancement by a potential adversary.' On collection: 'The UAPTF had no MASINT reporting on the events considered in this dataset' — which stands in direct tension with the later Immaculate Constellation allegation that a parent USAP holds high-quality IMINT and MASINT of UAP.

The redaction pattern is itself evidence. The FOIA version, approved for release on 24 March 2022 under case DF-2021-00275, still withholds material under (b)(1) — properly classified national defence information — and (b)(3), statutory exemption. The sentence identifying the accountable official reads, in the released copy, 'The UAPTF Director, is the official accountable for ensuring the timely collection and consolidation of data on UAP,' with the name removed. Passages describing unusual flight characteristics, GEOINT and SIGINT collection, and specific incidents are blank. The unclassified public product is therefore a curated fraction of what Congress received, and the delta is where the argument lives.

ODNI's second role is structural. Under 50 U.S.C. 3373 the Secretary of Defense must act 'in coordination with the Director of National Intelligence' in establishing AARO, and the reporting mechanism must be established 'in consultation with the Director of National Intelligence.' AARO is housed inside OUSD(I&S). And DoDD 5205.07, effective 12 September 2024 and approved by Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen Hicks, designates USD(I&S) as the office that 'serves as the primary interface for the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) and members of the Intelligence Community (IC), including sharing with the DoD compartmented capabilities and information intended for inclusion and subsequent apportionment.' In other words, the same office that hosts the body Congress created to find unreported UAP programs is the office through which IC compartmented capabilities are moved into and out of DoD special access programs. Whether that is an oversight design flaw or the point is the question the board exists to press.

The third role is the whistleblower channel. In 2022, while at the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, David Grusch filed a Presidential Policy Directive 19 urgent-concern complaint with the Intelligence Community Inspector General. Thomas Monheim, IC Inspector General from April 2020 to January 2025, found the complaint credible and urgent, and a summary went to the Director of National Intelligence and to the House and Senate intelligence committees. Grusch then testified publicly to House Oversight in July 2023. No ODNI product has since publicly addressed the substance of the referral.

Finally, ODNI has been the co-publisher of record for the successor reporting. The Fiscal Year 2024 Consolidated Annual Report on Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena, released 14 November 2024 the day after the House Oversight hearing, reported 757 UAP reports received, 485 of which occurred within the reporting period and 272 of which occurred in 2021-2022 but were reported late; 118 cases resolved to prosaic objects; 21 unresolved. That report is a DoD/AARO product carried on the ODNI website, and under this board's sourcing rules it is a primary record of what the government said, not of what is true.

What the record does not show is any ODNI statement about retrievals, materials, or reverse-engineering. There is no ODNI acknowledgement of a legacy program, and no public ODNI response to the Grusch referral.
openQuestions: Who is the UAPTF Director redacted under (b)(6) in the FOIA copy of the 2021 assessment?
What does the classified annex to the 2021 preliminary assessment contain, and who at ODNI has seen it?
What action, if any, did ODNI or the DNI take on the ICIG's credible-and-urgent referral of the Grusch complaint?
Has ODNI or any IC element transferred records to NARA Record Group 615, and what did they withhold?
Which ODNI element holds equity in any UAP-related compartmented capability shared with DoD SAPs through the USD(I&S) interface?
Why could the IC not deconflict its own UAP dataset against classified US aerospace programs — was the deconfliction attempted and refused, or never possible at the UAPTF's access level?
dossier.whatItIs: The Office of the Director of National Intelligence is the coordinating headquarters of the US Intelligence Community, created by the Intelligence Reform and Terrorism Prevention Act of 2004 and headed by the Director of National Intelligence. Since 2021 it has been the statutory co-owner of the government's UAP reporting machinery: it published the June 2021 'Preliminary Assessment: Unidentified Aerial Phenomena,' it is the office with which the Secretary of Defense must coordinate in establishing and running AARO, and it co-issues the annual consolidated UAP reports. Its Inspector General is also the channel through which UAP whistleblower complaints reach the congressional intelligence committees.
dossier.whyImplicated: ODNI sits on both sides of the ledger, and that is precisely what makes it useful. It is the office that publicly certified that most reported UAP 'probably do represent physical objects,' that eleven documented pilot near-misses exist, and — critically — that it could not confirm that any of the collected reports were attributable to classified US government or industry developmental programs. An intelligence headquarters that cannot deconflict a UAP dataset against its own black programs is either not being told, or is telling us it is not being told. At the same time, ODNI is the institutional counterparty for every DoD SAP that shares compartmented capabilities with the IC, and AARO is lodged inside the DoD office designated as ODNI's primary interface. Its Inspector General found David Grusch's complaint alleging concealed retrieval and reverse-engineering programs 'credible and urgent' and forwarded it to the DNI and both intelligence committees, after which nothing publicly followed. Even the FOIA-released version of its own 2021 assessment is redacted under (b)(1) and (b)(3), including the identity of the official it names as accountable.
